content: Patients who are co-infected with HIV and hepatitis C virus (HCV) and are receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART) alongside HCV treatment require careful monitoring. This is due to the potential for drug interactions and an increased risk of drug toxicity between certain HCV medications and antiretroviral (ARV) drugs. Detailed information on these interactions can be found in the latest WHO guidelines for the screening, care, and treatment of hepatitis C infection, as well as the consolidated guidelines on the use of ARV drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection. To improve access to ART for opioid-dependent people who inject drugs (PWID), the WHO recommends decentralizing ART initiation and maintenance to settings where opioid substitution therapy (OST) is provided. ART initiation at peripheral health facilities, with maintenance at the community level (e.g., outreach centers, health posts, home-based services, or community-based organizations), is also encouraged. Decentralization of ART services aims to enhance adherence. Addressing depression, managing drug and alcohol dependence, and providing peer support and patient education are essential components of HIV care and have been shown to improve treatment outcomes. Efforts to support adherence should begin before ART initiation, with the development of an adherence plan and patient education covering basic HIV information, ARV drugs, expected side effects, and preparation for treatment. Routine HIV testing should be offered to all patients with presumptive or diagnosed tuberculosis (TB). Community-based HTS linked to prevention, care, and treatment services is recommended for PWID, in addition to provider-initiated testing and counseling. In generalized epidemics, provider-initiated testing and counseling should be offered to everyone attending healthcare facilities, including those in TB, sexually transmitted infection (STI), and hepatitis clinics, as well as inpatient and outpatient settings. In concentrated or low-level epidemics, testing should be considered in services for STIs, hepatitis, and TB, as well as for PWID. Effective referral systems are an alternative but require proactive follow-up and consideration of patient barriers such as transportation costs and time constraints. Patients should be closely monitored for side effects related to co-treatment of TB, HIV, and drug dependence, as well as for TB-associated immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS), which is common but usually self-limiting. Preventive therapy with co-trimoxazole (CPT) should be provided to all HIV-infected TB patients, regardless of CD4 count, as part of the HIV chronic care package. CPT is a cost-effective intervention that reduces mortality and morbidity by preventing secondary bacterial and parasitic infections. HIV and TB programs should establish systems to provide CPT to all eligible PWID living with HIV who have active TB. HIV prevention for PWID should include access to sterile injecting equipment through needle and syringe programs (NSPs), consistent and correct condom use with compatible lubricants, and periodic screening for asymptomatic STIs. Comprehensive prevention strategies should also address safer drug use, protected sex, and knowledge of HIV status. Opioid substitution therapy (OST) with methadone or buprenorphine is the most effective pharmacological treatment for opioid dependence. It reduces HIV and viral hepatitis risk behaviors, supports adherence to ART and TB treatment, and improves clinical outcomes. OST should be provided in adequate doses and for sufficient duration, with flexible dosing policies to maximize safety and effectiveness. Psychosocial support should be routinely offered alongside pharmacological treatment for opioid dependence. Pregnant patients with opioid dependence should be advised to continue or commence OST. Naloxone should be made available to individuals likely to witness an opioid overdose, with training on its administration for emergency management. Collaboration between HIV, TB, and drug dependence treatment services is essential to prevent interruptions in therapy and to provide a stable continuum of care.
